newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania port to reopen after unrest.
newsitem.headline: Albania port to reopen after unrest.

text.p: Albania's second port of Vlore could reopen in days despite continuing lawlessness in the town, the epicentre of the country's recent unrest.

Italian and Greek soldiers from a multinational security force have secured the port that closed nearly three months ago when Albanians angered over the collapse of savings funds took to the streets, clashing with the police and army.
By day shops, cafes and small businesses are open in Vlore and police patrol the streets, but at night armed gangs rule.
"We are trying to reopen the port to put some life back into trading activities here," Medin Xhelili, chairman of the district council, told Reuters on Thursday.
"We have had confirmation from the multinational force that there is no problem for security and boats can come under watch of the troops. It is just a matter of days."
Xhelili said the town still had major problems: banks were burnt down during the crisis and pensioners have to collect their money from the police station.
Electricity and water services are operating as normal but schools have yet to reopen and cleaning and sewage services are a problem in some areas.
"The number of guns around makes the situation very difficult. We have people trying to steal or revenge old grudges that now act with guns," he said.
At night in Vlore the sound of gunfire echoes across the harbour aqnd tracers light up the sky.
The police can do nothing or disarm the thousands of Vlore residents who have armed themselves from state arsenals for self-protection or to stop the armed gangs that rule after nightfall.

"We cannot act in these conditions. The courts are not working, the prosecutor's office is not working and the police force is not strong enough or adequately equipped," Milto Kordha, the head of Vlore's police force, told Reuters.
"At the moment we cannot stop them," said Kordha, who has asked the interim government in Tirana for more men and equipment.
Two men were killed and two injured overnight Wednesday in a car chase in the outskirts of the town. A 23-year old man died after shooting himself accidentally.
Three police officers were killed a month ago in a car chase with an armed car thief.
"These bandits pose as patriots. They have come back from abroad saying they are coming back to help Vlore, restore law and order and help the people," Kordha said.

He said Vlore citizens, grouped in a so-called salvation committee to help the chaotic town and to demand the return of money from pyramid schemes, were working for the good of Vlore and were not linked to the armed gangs.
The salvation committees demand the resignation of President Sali Berisha, who they blame for doing nothing to prevent the pyramid disaster.
Berisha has accused the committees of being the armed wing of the opposition Socialist Party which will face his Democratic Party in a general election expected on June 29.
The president has demanded the Vlore salvation committee, and similar associations in other southern Albanian towns, disband before the election.
Albert Shyti, the head of the Vlore salvation committee, denied any political motive.
"We have no relationship at all with any of the political parties," Shyti told Reuters in an interview at the committee's headquarters in a disused town centre school.
"The committees want to help local government...but also we want our money back."
